title: What Are Fossil Fuels? Coal, Oil, Gas and Energy Units
excerpt: Learn what fossil fuels are, how coal, oil and natural gas differ, and how to compare energy, power, efficiency, costs and emissions using clear examples.
content:
**Fossil fuels are coal, petroleum and natural gas: energy resources formed from ancient organic material over geological time.** They are nonrenewable on human timescales. Understanding them requires more than remembering three names; it also means distinguishing the fuel itself, the energy converted from it and the useful service supplied to a household, vehicle or factory.

This student guide uses the U.S. Energy Information Administration's educational explanations for definitions and unit distinctions, checked on 23 November 2026. All numerical classroom examples below are hypothetical. They are not Pakistan fuel prices, a current national electricity mix or performance claims about a named power station.

## Why are coal, petroleum and natural gas called fossil fuels?

The term refers to their origin in ancient organic material, rather than to a requirement that a visible fossil be present in a fuel sample. The resources have undergone natural processes over very long periods. The resulting materials can be extracted and used in energy systems.

Coal is commonly encountered as a solid fuel, petroleum as a liquid resource processed into products, and natural gas as a gaseous fuel. Those ordinary descriptions help identify their forms, but they do not imply that every sample has identical composition or energy content. Commercial specifications and measurement conditions still matter.

The distinction between a resource and a product is especially useful for petroleum. A crude-oil resource is not the same object as a finished motor fuel sold under a particular specification. A comparison should identify what material it is discussing rather than using oil, petrol and every petroleum product interchangeably.

For a classroom classification activity, write resource, processed product and delivered service in separate columns. Place each example in the appropriate column and explain the choice. The activity encourages students to follow a system rather than treating every familiar energy-related word as another name for the same thing.

## What does nonrenewable actually mean?

Nonrenewable describes the relationship between a resource's formation and its use. Fossil-fuel supplies are not replenished at a rate that matches ordinary human consumption. This is a statement about the nature of the resource, not a precise countdown announcing when every deposit will disappear.

An estimate of recoverable resources also depends on what is known and what can be extracted under stated conditions. A headline naming an amount should identify its source, reference date and definition. Do not treat every estimate labelled resources or reserves as the same measurement.

Nor does nonrenewable mean fossil fuel. EIA classifies nuclear energy separately from fossil fuels while discussing uranium among nonrenewable resources. The two categories answer different questions: one concerns replenishment, while the other concerns the origin and type of the fuel.

Write two questions on a revision card: how is the resource formed, and is it replenished on a relevant human timescale? Answering both produces a more useful classification than memorising a single list. It also prevents an exam answer from claiming that every nonrenewable resource is coal, oil or gas.

## How does a fuel differ from electricity?

A fuel stores energy that can be converted in a process. Electricity is a secondary energy source or carrier produced from primary sources. A socket does not reveal which primary sources supplied the electricity reaching it, and the same electrical device can operate on electricity generated through different systems.

Consider the chain fuel, conversion equipment, electricity network and appliance. Each stage performs a different role. A statement about the fuel going into a power station is not automatically a statement about the amount of useful service delivered by an appliance at the end of the chain.

This distinction also explains why a comparison needs a boundary. Are you comparing primary energy supplied to generating equipment, electricity leaving the station, electricity delivered to a building or useful light produced by a lamp? Different boundaries can produce different figures without either figure being an arithmetic error.

Draw the stages as labelled boxes in your notes. Put the measured quantity beside the relevant box or arrow. If a source does not identify its measurement boundary, record that limitation before comparing it with another source that uses a clearly different stage of the system.

## What is the difference between energy and power?

Energy describes an amount, while power describes the rate at which energy is transferred or converted. Kilowatts and kilowatt-hours therefore measure different quantities. A kilowatt-hour is an energy unit; it is not a complicated way of writing a kilowatt.

For a hypothetical device drawing a constant **2 kilowatts for 3 hours**, the electrical energy used is **2 × 3 = 6 kilowatt-hours**. The calculation multiplies power by time. Real equipment can vary its draw, so an actual consumption estimate should use a measured or appropriately averaged power value.

A different hypothetical device drawing 1 kilowatt for 6 hours also uses 6 kilowatt-hours under the stated constant-power assumption. Equal energy totals do not establish equal power demand. The timing of the demand and the service supplied can still differ.

Label every number in a worked answer. If a student writes only 6, the reader cannot tell whether it represents kilowatts, hours or kilowatt-hours. Keeping the units in the equation is a practical way to catch an invalid operation before trusting the final result.

## Why cannot litres, tonnes and kilowatt-hours simply be added?

A litre is a volume measurement, a tonne is a mass measurement and a kilowatt-hour is an energy measurement. Adding their numerical values does not create a meaningful energy total. A comparison needs compatible quantities and a documented method for conversion.

Suppose a fictional exercise assigns Fuel A an energy content of 10 units per litre and Fuel B 20 units per kilogram. Three litres of A represent 30 energy units, while two kilograms of B represent 40. Their combined energy is 70 units under those invented factors, not five units because three plus two equals five.

The example is deliberately abstract. It is not a conversion table for petrol, gas or coal. Real factors depend on the particular fuel and the conditions represented by the source. EIA's unit guidance explains why fuel comparisons use energy conversion factors rather than treating all physical units as interchangeable.

When using a published conversion factor, copy its unit, date and stated basis with the value. A number stripped of those details may look convenient in a spreadsheet but can make a later calculation impossible to audit or reproduce accurately.

## How should efficiency be calculated?

An efficiency calculation compares a defined useful output with a corresponding input. The input and output should be expressed in compatible energy units and measured across the same stated boundary. The result is a ratio, usually expressed as a percentage.

In a fictional conversion process, 100 energy units enter and 35 units leave in the specified useful form. The stated efficiency is **35 ÷ 100 × 100 = 35 percent**. The remaining 65 units are outside that defined useful output; the calculation does not claim that energy has ceased to exist.

Now imagine another process delivering 40 useful units from the same 100-unit input. Its efficiency under that definition is 40 percent. The increase from 35 to 40 is **5 percentage points**. Relative to the original 35, the proportional increase is approximately 14.3 percent. These are different comparisons.

An efficiency label without a boundary can be misleading. Ask what counts as useful output and which inputs were counted. Do not compare two percentages merely because both appear beside energy equipment; first confirm that they describe compatible processes and definitions.

## How do capacity and actual generation differ?

A power-capacity figure describes a rate, while a generation figure records energy produced over a period. A large capacity number does not by itself establish how much electricity was generated on a particular day. The duration and actual operation must also be known.

For a hypothetical generator producing a constant 5 megawatts for 4 hours, output is **20 megawatt-hours**. If it operates for only 2 hours at that output, the corresponding energy is 10 megawatt-hours. These are classroom calculations, not observations about any country's grid.

This helps explain why an installed-capacity share and an electricity-generation share need not be equal. One describes the distribution of rated power, while the other describes output over a chosen period. Neither should be relabelled as the other to make two charts appear consistent.

When reading a chart, write the measured quantity, the unit and the period above your notes. If the chart has a percentage axis, also identify the denominator. A percentage of capacity, generation, primary-energy use or expenditure answers a different question even if the same fuel names appear.

## How should students compare costs without inventing a tariff?

Separate the amount of energy from its price per unit. In a fictional exercise, 6 kilowatt-hours priced at 10 currency units per kilowatt-hour cost 60 currency units for that energy component. The assumed price is not a current electricity tariff or a prediction of a household bill.

Actual bills can include other components and rules. A basic multiplication exercise does not establish all those components, nor does it establish the retail price of a fuel merely because an international commodity price is available. Keep the scope of the calculation explicit.

If a comparison uses different fuels, establish the delivered energy or useful service being purchased before ranking the prices. A cheap physical unit can contain a different amount of energy from another unit. Conversion and process assumptions can therefore change the interpretation of a price comparison.

For a worksheet, supply the price and energy-content assumptions in the question itself. Ask students to show the units at each step and to state what the final answer excludes. That makes the exercise assess reasoning without pretending to provide current financial guidance.

## What should an emissions comparison specify?

An emissions figure needs a named substance, a quantity, a period and a system boundary. Carbon dioxide emissions from combustion are not the same measurement as every environmental effect associated with extracting, processing and transporting a fuel. A clear comparison identifies what has actually been counted.

EIA's greenhouse-gas explanation provides background on the gases discussed in energy reporting. For a student exercise, keep the gas label attached to the figure. Do not replace a specific substance with a vague pollution total or assume that two differently defined measures can be compared directly.

Consider a purely hypothetical dataset in which Activity A emits 20 mass units while delivering 10 service units, and Activity B emits 30 mass units while delivering 30 service units. Their intensities are respectively 2 and 1 mass units per service unit. B has a larger total but a lower intensity in this invented example.

Neither the total nor the intensity is automatically the only useful measure. The question determines which is relevant. Reporting both, with their units and assumptions, prevents a comparison from concealing the scale of activity or confusing a rate with an absolute amount.

## How can a chart about energy become misleading?

Start with the title, axes, legend, geography and period. A chart about one country's electricity generation does not establish the world's total energy use. A monthly observation does not automatically describe an annual trend. Read those labels before interpreting the shape of the bars.

Percentage changes also require a starting value. An invented increase from 10 to 15 is a rise of five units and a 50 percent increase relative to 10. An increase from 100 to 105 is also five units but only five percent relative to 100. Equal absolute changes need not represent equal proportional changes.

If a graph omits its baseline or changes the vertical scale between panels, note that presentation choice before comparing the apparent size of movements. The underlying values and the visual impression can tell different stories, especially when readers see only a cropped screenshot.

Use the original table when available and reproduce one calculation independently. A small arithmetic check cannot validate an entire dataset, but it can reveal a transcription mistake, a mismatched denominator or a percentage computed from the wrong reference value.

## What is a useful fossil-fuel revision exercise?

Make a four-part worksheet. First classify coal, petroleum, natural gas, electricity and nuclear energy using the distinctions above. Next label the stages of a fictional energy-conversion chain. Then solve one power-times-time question and one efficiency question with the assumptions supplied explicitly.

For the final part, compare two fictional totals and intensities and explain why they answer different questions. Require a sentence naming the measurement boundary in each answer. This tests whether the student understands the quantities rather than only remembering a list of resources.

Our [air-pollution guide](/blogs/air-pollution-pm25-aqi-student-guide/) provides a related exercise in distinguishing measurements. Energy use, an emissions total and a local air-quality indicator should not be treated as the same variable. Each requires its own definition and evidence.

The central habit is simple: name the material, identify the measured quantity, preserve its unit and state the conditions of the comparison. That method makes fossil-fuel questions easier to answer and helps readers interpret energy headlines without inventing current prices, national statistics or equipment performance.
